newsitem.title: USA: CBOT wheat closes higher on U.S., European weather.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat closes higher on U.S., European weather.

text.p: Harsh winter-like weather during springtime in the U.S. plus dry weather in Europe boosted CBOT wheat futures to a strongly higher close, traders said.

"We do have dynamics changing quite a bit for wheat," said Bob Lekberg, grains and oilseed analyst for Chicago-based trade house Goldenberg Hehmeyer. "There's a potential disruption in plantings in the northern U.S. spring wheat area and cold weather is coming into the (hard red) winter area."
Portions of the HRW crop is vulnerable to winterkill.
Much of the wheat in the HRW states is at the jointing stage, in which the seed-producing head of the plant starts moving up stalks called tillers. A severe freeze now would kill the tillers.
"What likely will happen is the tillers jointing now will be killed," said Gary Paulsen, an agronomy professor at Kansas State University in Manhattan, Kansas.
Goldenberg Hehmeyer bought nine million bushels of the July. The purchase was said done for a commercial firm.
Wheat closed one to 10-1/2 cents per bushel higher, with May up 10 at $4.03 and July up 10-1/4 at $4.08-1/4.

Weather Services Corp early Friday forecast potentially- damaging cold Sunday morning with low temperatures possibly falling to 18 to 25 degrees Fahrenheit in the northern Plains and 25 to 35 in the southern Plains. WSC also forecast patchy light snow and rain in the Plains Friday, which could protect some of the crop from harm.
Traders also cited potential dry-weather stress to the European wheat crop as central to Friday's rally.
London traders Friday said the dry weather has been the main obsession of European grain traders this week and looks set to hold center stage, with no significant rain forecast.
"There's a lot of talk about the dry conditions in Europe. It's rapidly becoming a world weather market again down here," a trader said.
Earlier this week, the French government ordered farmers in the Beauce, Europe's biggest grain-producing region, to reduce irrigation of their crops due to early signs of drought.

Mild support in wheat futures also stemmed from USDA's Supply/Demand Report released early Friday. USDA cut its estimate for 1996-97 U.S. wheat ending stocks to 460 million bushels from its previous estimate of 474 million bushels. The wheat marketing year ends May 31.
In spread trading, SAK Futures did 400,000 July/May at 4-1/2 cents, premium July and Cargill Investor Services did 200,000 July/May at 4-1/2 cents, premium July, traders said.

In addition to its purchase of nine million July, Goldenberg Hehmeyer bought three million May, traders said. Cargill Inc bought four million bushels of September, Merrill Lynch Futures bought two million July and Refco Inc bought 2.5 million bushels of July and Smith Barney bought two million bushels of July, traders said. Funds bought at least 20 million bushels of wheat Friday, traders said.
Wheat futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 35,000 contracts, above the 25,965 traded Thursday.
In wheat options, Tenco Inc sold 200 July $4.10 puts at 22 cents and sold 200 September $4.20 puts at 51-1/2 cents, traders said.
Wheat options volume was estimated at 15,000 contracts, below the 17,512 traded Thursday.
